#3277. Not Nvidia. Not Palantir. The Midterms Just Made This Magnificent Artificial Intelligence (AI) Stock the Safer Bet.

The Democratic Party won control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate in the midterm elections.

The 2026 midterm elections ended in a major political shake-up, with Democrats winning control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate. While the results do not necessarily change the long-term outlook for artificial intelligence (AI), they could introduce new risks for some of the market's most popular AI stocks.

Companies such as Nvidia (NVDA -9.26%) and Palantir Technologies (PLTR -9.73%) have benefited enormously from the AI revolution so far. However, potential changes to federal spending priorities and greater scrutiny of AI infrastructure could complicate their growth trajectories going forward.

For investors looking to capitalize on the AI theme without taking on quite as much uncertainty, I think Microsoft (MSFT -3.58%) offers an interesting alternative.

Nvidia has become the backbone of the AI infrastructure boom. The company's graphics processing units (GPUs) power many of the data centers being built by Amazon (AMZN -2.19%), Microsoft, Alphabet (GOOGL -2.20%) (GOOG -1.93%), and Meta Platforms (META -3.96%).

However, data centers have become a political issue, particularly regarding electricity consumption, utility costs, and the strain on local infrastructure. Should the incoming Democratic Congress pursue tougher oversight or legislation affecting data center build-outs, hyperscalers could face higher development costs or longer approval timelines. In turn, this could cause big tech to reevaluate the pace of their infrastructure investments, potentially impacting demand for Nvidia's chips.

Palantir faces a different type of uncertainty. During the third quarter, the company generated $1.15 billion in government revenue, representing about half of its total sales. Although the company's commercial business is expanding rapidly, government contracting remains a key tailwind. If lawmakers pursue different defense spending priorities, Palantir could face a more challenging environment for securing new business from the public sector.

Microsoft is not completely immune to these risks. The company operates one of the top three largest cloud computing businesses in the world and is also investing heavily in AI infrastructure. However, what separates Microsoft from Nvidia and Palantir is the diversity of its revenue streams and business model.

Through Azure, Microsoft benefits directly from accelerating demand for AI compute. Meanwhile, products such as Microsoft 365, Windows, Dynamics, and cybersecurity software help generate additional recurring revenue. This means Microsoft can monetize AI through software subscriptions and enterprise productivity tools, even if the pace of data center construction eventually moderates. There is also an interesting regulatory distinction between Microsoft and its hyperscaler peers.

Amazon has faced an antitrust lawsuit from the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) since 2023, with regulators alleging that its online marketplace practices unfairly restrict competing e-commerce platforms and harm third-party sellers. Google has faced its share of legal setbacks, including a recent federal court ruling that it illegally monopolized certain digital advertising markets.

Meanwhile, Meta's regulatory challenges date back to a 2020 FTC lawsuit alleging that its acquisitions of Instagram and WhatsApp were designed to eliminate emerging competitors in the social media landscape. Although Meta won in court last November, the FTC appealed that decision in January -- keeping the dispute alive.

Microsoft has certainly faced regulatory scrutiny as well, including an investigation by the European Commission into bundling Teams with Microsoft 365. Still, I think its broad enterprise software ecosystem makes it an attractive way to invest in AI without relying as heavily on digital advertising or consumer platforms. While Microsoft is not politically untouchable, its combination of cloud infrastructure, established software properties, and recurring enterprise subscriptions offers multiple avenues for growth.

Microsoft's latest earnings results illustrate why its business model is so attractive. During its fiscal first quarter of 2027 (ended Sept. 30), revenue increased 19% year over year to $92.3 billion. Azure revenue soared 48%, while Microsoft Cloud revenue climbed 30% to $63.9 billion.

Even more impressive, Microsoft's commercial remaining performance obligations (RPO) increased 73% to $677 billion. This figure represents contracted business that has yet to be recognized as revenue, providing meaningful visibility into future sales.

The company's cash flow is another important consideration. Microsoft generated $58 billion in operating cash flow during the quarter, increasing 29% year over year. However, capital expenditures (capex) totaled $45.2 billion, reflecting the enormous costs of building AI infrastructure. This means Microsoft generated roughly $18.6 billion in free cash flow during the quarter, illustrating how data center investments are consuming a meaningful portion of its cash generation.

This creates an interesting potential upside scenario: If Microsoft moderates its infrastructure spending while continuing to monetize its existing cloud capacity and software ecosystem, free cash flow could improve substantially.

From a valuation perspective, Microsoft trades at a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of about 27 following the election. While this is hardly a bargain in absolute terms, I think it's a reasonable premium for a company delivering double-digit revenue growth, expanding AI-driven cloud adoption, and generating recurring cash flow.

With a changing political landscape creating more uncertainty around infrastructure spending and federal contracts, Microsoft strikes me as a more balanced AI investment right now. For investors with a long-term time horizon, Microsoft may be one of the safer AI stocks to own following the midterms.

Currently inside Settings ⇾ Screen Saver you’ll find four categories:

Follow this ultimate checklist before the frost hits

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

My yard is absolutely covered in leaves and that's always one of the biggest indicators that I need to start seriously thinking about getting it ready for winter. The winter months bring their own set of challenges from thinning grass to damaged roots, so being prepared and protecting your shrubs and lawn will ultimately save you a lot of time, money and hard work.

Over the past few years, I've streamlined the steps I take in order to fit in my winter garden prep before it gets too cold and before the frost starts to wreak havoc on my plants. Here's the 5-step checklist I swear by each year to get my yard winter ready.

As mentioned, the fallen leaves are the first problem I know I need to tackle. They can quickly damage the glass, blocking sunlight and reducing air circulation. Once I've raked up the leaves with my favorite 'tarp burrito' method, I need to focus on removing any more debris and clutter.

Over the summer months, my yard has been lovingly used, but that means there are tools, toys and leftover gardening items lying around. For winter, it's important to clear up and pack away everything that doesn't belong. Not only because leaving them out will damage your yard, but it'll ruin the items too.

It's hard to pick plants for your yard that last all-year round and some in particular are sensitive to the winter weather, especially those which are tropical/exotic. After you identify which plants these are, it's a great idea to wrap them up to protect them. For this, I look to the 5 household items that can protect your plants from frost.

My personal favorites to use are horticultural fleece or bubble wrap as it's something I usually have leftover from the year before (or ready for wrapping presents in the holiday season). As soon as the temperature really drops or there's warning of frost, I like to wrap them up and leave them until spring.

This large fleece is specifically designed to protect outdoor plants from the cold weather. Available in three sizes, it also comes with the pegs needed to pin and secure the fleece into the ground. Importantly, it's also breathable material meaning your plants will still manage to survive underneath.

Working out when to give your lawn one last mow depends on where you're living, but it also shouldn't just be dictated because you know you're heading into the winter months. As the Farmers' Almanac explains: "Keep mowing your lawn as long as the grass is actively growing." And that's a rule I live by.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Adding: "A useful temperature clue is when daytime high temperatures consistently remain near or below 50°F." But you also shouldn't go on temperature alone. Consider the growth, temperature and type of grass you have in your yard as well – and, of course, whether it's still growing.

Another way to protect the plants before the winter hits is to apply some compost or bark mulch around the roots. This works as a great insulator to protect them from frost, as well as protecting the soil in general which can deteriorate during extreme winds and heavy rains.

As a rule, I like to add about a 2 to 3 inch layer as a sort of winter blanket that mimics the one I find myself sitting under. This is also an effective way to stop weeds that are hardy enough to penetrate the soil from growing all winter long.

In the same way I like to clear up any debris or clutter in my yard, I think it's also important to focus on any lawn, yard or patio furniture you've been putting to good use over the summer months.

It's far too easy when it gets cold and dark outside to forget about the furniture and put off clearing it up or covering it over for another day. If you keep forgetting, you're putting your furniture in danger of rust, excessive wear or even rotting. So, get out there and get it wrapped up before it's too late!

Oily pans, stews and sauces are no match for the bread sponge trick.

If you want to degrease a pan or the top layer of an oily sauce without ruining a sponge, a single slice of bread could be your new favorite cleaning sidekick.

While we have vastly improved how we dispose of most things, excess cooking grease still presents a problem. Down the sink? Not advisable. Neither is the dishwasher—even the garbage bin can become a gnarly affair.

Getting the bulk of the grease out of a pan after cooking a batch of bacon or burgers is a good first step, but that greasy pan will either take down a sponge or half a roll of paper towels. What if a humble slice of past-its-prime sandwich bread was the all-natural solution for greasy pans you’ve been looking for?

It’s cheap and easy, and you can toss the used-up bread into a compost bin or countertop food waste processor without disrupting its yuck-free operation.

So, is it ever OK to pour excess grease or used cooking oil down the sink? Even if you run the hot water tap at the same time? Short answer: no. Long answer? Here’s an expert for the “no.” “When grease cools, it solidifies, coating the interior of the pipe,” says Jacylyn Basilone, chief operating officer of Brooks Plumbing. Even if you’re running hot water, the grease will eventually cool further down the line and cause future problems. “Over time, the solidified grease in the pipes can catch debris, thus making a partial clog grow larger and larger,” she says, reducing the pipe’s circumference little by little if you do this repeatedly.

Unlike a clogged shower drain, which you can usually clear easily, “a normal sewer machine or ‘snake’ can’t alleviate this type of stoppage,” says Basilone. “While grease solidifies, it can’t be captured by the claw head. Grease removal is best remediated with a hydrojetter, which tends to be more expensive than the traditional drain-cleaning services.”

Bread is the real answer, and I can’t believe I haven’t been doing this all along. (*Hangs head in shame, fully guilty of relying on the obviously very sketchy hot water method.*)

Bread has always been a superb grease-mopping tool; we usually think of it in a culinary context rather than for waste removal. Just as you’d drag a crusty baguette or hunk of ciabatta across the drippings on your plate, bread is an excellent sponge for all manner of oil, whether or not it is appealing to consume. Using bread to soak up excess oil essentially turns liquid food waste into a solid, making disposal much easier.

If it’s not obvious, this is also a great way to use bread that might otherwise go to waste: the ends of the loaf you can’t bring yourself to eat, or bread that’s gone stale or is starting to show the first mold spores. If you’re going to discard the bread anyway, at least put it to good use.

The bread trick comes in handy in almost endless ways. If there’s a pool of oil, it’s the mop for the job. I initially tried it after cooking bacon. A single, small slice of bread was enough to absorb what was easily four to six ounces of liquid grease left in the pan. I dragged the slice around the pan like a mop, but even after letting it sit a few extra moments, it kept working and eventually soaked up all the liquid grease. (If you’re feeling indulgent and used a fresh bread slice for this purpose, the temptation to make pretty epic croutons here is quite strong — another upside.)

If your air fryer has space between the drawer and the basket, you can place the bread there to soak up grease while cooking. Even for oily, slow-cooked proteins like pork shoulder, you can press the bread onto the meat to soak up grease before serving.

Once the bread has absorbed the oil and needs discarding, responsible food-waste methods are much easier to manage. Depending on how much oil the bread has absorbed, you can safely put the soaked bread in the compost bin or countertop composter without risking a major oil spill and a mess to clean up later. Oil can slow decomposition, so composting large amounts isn’t recommended. Small amounts, such as a few tablespoons at a time, are safe.

Even if you have no other option but to throw it away — and if that is the case, please consider getting a small composting appliance — at the very least, you’re not involving an easily recyclable glass container.

For more home tips, learn this neat trick for reusing frying oil and learn the 10 worst things to pour down your drain.

Having the right context is what makes AI tools useful. Anthropic just launched the ability to securely use personal finance data with Claude. The company emphasizes that the feature is read-only and can’t take financial actions.

Your weekend watchlist, including 'Black Doves,' 'Primetime' and 'Stick'

November has arrived, which means holiday season is starting to peek around the corner. Before the festive movies completely take over, there's still plenty of time to enjoy a good thriller, an underdog sports story or some zombie-fueled mayhem. The best new movies and shows to watch this weekend are arriving on Netflix, Prime Video, Apple TV and other streaming services, as well as broadcast and cable.

As Tom's Guide's streaming editor, I've rounded up and ranked this week's biggest releases to help you spend less time scrolling and more time watching. "Black Doves" season 2 brings back the deadly espionage and messy double lives, while "Stick" season 2 tees up another round of unlikely sports redemption. Over on the movie front, let Robert Pattinson creep you out as Chris Hansen in "Primetime," or sink into the video game thrills of "Resident Evil." Then, there's "A Dog's First Christmas," which offers a decidedly fluffier and cheerful alternative.

So grab a blanket, pour something warm (or break out the first holiday mug of the season) and settle in. Here's what to watch this weekend, ranked by must-watch factor.

Kelly recently reviewed "Black Doves" season 2 and "The Gilded Age" season 4.

Genre: Spy thrillerAvailable now: All 6 episodes (about 1 hour each)What it's about: Keira Knightley returns as Helen Webb, the seemingly respectable wife of a rising political star who moonlights as an informant for a shadowy spy organization. With husband Wallace (Andrew Buchan) eyeing the prime minister's office, Helen has even more to lose if her double life comes to light. Meanwhile, her handler Mrs. Reed (Sarah Lancashire) is fighting off a threat of her own, and old pal Sam (Ben Whishaw) is back in the picture, ready to make trouble.Why you should watch it: The first season was a killer combination of slick spycraft, pitch-black humor and complicated friendships. Season 2 looks ready to deliver more of the same, with Knightley and Whishaw's crackling chemistry and Lancashire's deliciously inscrutable operator adding plenty of intrigue. Where to watch: Netflix

Genre: Biographical sports dramaAvailable now: All 8 episodes (about 55 min each)What it's about: Before he became Muhammad Ali, he was Cassius Clay (Jaalen Best), a young boxer with Olympic gold, heavyweight ambitions and a mouth that could knock you out before he even entered the ring. The series traces his rise from promising fighter to global phenomenon, including his complicated relationship with his father (Omari Hardwick), his embrace of Islam and his friendship with Malcolm X (Michael Ealy).Why it's worth your time: You've heard the greatest call himself that. Now get to know the man behind the bravado. The looks beyond the legendary fights to the family conflicts and personal convictions that helped forge an icon.Where to watch: Prime Video

Genre: Psychological thrillerRuntime: 1 hour 49 minWhat it's about: Robert Pattinson stars as NBC journalist Chris Hansen, host of the controversial reality series “To Catch a Predator,” which lured suspected child predators into televised sting operations. But as Hansen and ambitious producer Andie Bender (Merritt Wever) chase bigger ratings, their pursuit of justice starts looking more like a witch hunt.Why you should watch it: Director Lance Oppenheim turns a real-life media scandal into a stylized, neo-gothic nightmare. Pattinson is deliciously unsettling as Hansen, a man seemingly giddy at the prospect of publicly humiliating his targets. It's a queasy, hypnotic takedown of reality TV's appetite for outrage, with a chilling reminder that the people behind the cameras can be just as scary as the ones in front of them.Where to watch: Prime Video (with purchase)

Genre: Survival horrorRuntime: 1 hour 34 minWhat it’s about: One very bad night in Raccoon City is about to get considerably worse. Austin Abrams stars as Bryan, an ordinary medical courier tasked with delivering a mysterious package to a remote hospital. But after a car accident leaves him stranded in a city crawling with mutated monsters, his delivery becomes a desperate fight to stay alive. Bryan will need to complete a series of near-impossible missions to make it through the night.Why you should watch it:Director Zach Cregger (“Weapons,” “Barbarian”) delivers a lean, mean horror ride packed with grotesque creatures, action-packed set pieces and just enough dark humor. This is not the most faithful of “Resident Evil” adaptations, so you don't need to know the game lore to enjoy the carnage.Where to watch: Prime Video (with purchase)

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Genre: Sports comedyAvailable now: 2 episodes (about 30 min each)What it's about: Pryce Cahill (Owen Wilson) isn't content with being the guy behind the next golf superstar. After helping teenage phenom Santi (Peter Dager) get his career rolling, Pryce decides to dust off his own clubs and attempt an unlikely return to the pros. His target? Becoming the oldest golfer to win the U.S. Open. Why it's worth your time: Wilson has perfected his shaggy underdog mode, and he plays well opposite Timothy Olyphant as a rival pushing him along. Plus, Rhea Seehorn joins this season as a brutally honest swing coach. You don't get a cast much better than this.Where to watch: Apple TV

Genre: ComedyAvailable now: 1 episode (about 22 min)What it's about: Tracy Morgan returns as Reggie Dinkins, a disgraced former football star still chasing a career comeback with the help of documentary filmmaker Arthur Tobin (Daniel Radcliffe). But Reggie has fresh headaches to contend with, including his ex-wife Monica's (Erika Alexander) handsome new millionaire boyfriend.Why it's worth your time: With "30 Rock" alums Robert Carlock, Sam Means and Tina Fey behind the scenes, this sitcom has an impressive comedy pedigree. Morgan and Radcliffe make a great odd couple, and season 2 also brings a mini "30 Rock" reunion, with Jane Krakowski and Scott Adsit among the guest stars. Where to watch: Peacock

Genre: Supernatural horrorPremiere date: Episode 1 on Sunday, Nov. 8 at 9 p.m. ETWhat it's about: The kids have escaped the Institute, but their troubles are hardly over. Luke Ellis (Joe Freeman) and his fellow survivors are determined to bring the sinister operation down for good. Meanwhile, the Director is plotting a comeback with help from eccentric tech billionaire Nolan Reeves (Alfie Allen), while fugitive Ms. Sigsby (Mary-Louise Parker) is desperate to get back in the game.Why it's worth your time: Stephen King’s twisted tale of gifted kids and the adults who exploit them is officially going off-book. With a fresh storyline, a new villainous billionaire and plenty of unfinished business, season 2 has room to get even stranger. Where to watch: MGM+

Genre: ComedyAvailable now: All 8 episodes (about 25 min each)What it's about: Siaja (Anna Lambe) has worked hard to reinvent herself after blowing up her marriage, but independence comes with its own complications. Now running Ice Cove's research office, she's also grappling with the discovery of a long-lost sister and what it means for her family. Why it's worth your time: This warmhearted Canadian comedy finds plenty of laughs in the messy business of starting over and the antics of a very samll town. Consider this your invitation to get cozy in the Arctic.Where to watch: Netflix

Genre: Christmas comedy-dramaWhat it's about: Two Christmases after losing his wife, grumpy grandfather Sander (Dennis Quaid) is still struggling with grief, while his teen granddaughter Ello (Brooke Lena Johnson) is running out of patience. When a medical emergency leaves Ello's mother in an induced coma, it's up to Winstead, the family's wise old basset hound, and Ruby, an adorable Corgi puppy, to bring everyone back together.Why you should watch it: If adorable dogs and sentimental sappiness are your idea of Christmas cheer, Netflix has you covered. The streamer kicks off its holiday movie slate with this adaptation of the novel by “A Dog's Purpose” author W. Bruce Cameron. Also starring Milo Ventimiglia, Jennifer Tilly and Mary Steenburgen, it doesn’t reinvent the Christmas movie, but who cares when there’s a cute Corgi around?Where to watch: Netflix

Genre: Adult animated sci-fi WesternAvailable now: All 6 episodes (about 35 min each)What it's about: The Wild West gets a sci-fi makeover in this animated adventure starring Brian Tyree Henry as Bass Reeves, a lawman with a cybernetic arm and a whole lot of trouble on his hands. In a frontier crawling with vicious outlaws, rogue machines, and supernatural nasties, Bass must dispense justice while keeping his family out of the crossfire.Why it's worth your time: If your ideal Western involves robot mayhem and anime-style shootouts, saddle up for this series, which boasts gorgeous, kinetic animation and a badass Black hero (all too rare).Where to watch: Netflix

Genre: Legal dramaAvailable now: 3 episodes (about 45 min each)What it's about: Kim Kardashian returns as Allura Grant, the high-powered divorce attorney whose biggest challenge might be keeping her own house in order. Alongside partners Liberty Ronson (Naomi Watts) and Emerald Greene (Niecy Nash-Betts), she's navigating shifting loyalties, personal entanglements and a shocking revelation that threatens to take down their all-female law firm.Why it's worth your time: "All Fair" returns with another generous helping of scandal, designer wardrobes and people making bad personal decisions. Kim K may be the lead, but Glenn Close and Sarah Paulson are the real scenery-chewers.Where to watch: Hulu

Genre: Food and travel documentaryAvailable now: All 6 episodes (about 30 min each)What it's about: Awkwafina (aka Nora Lum) has a pretty impressive family legacy to live up to: Her great-grandfather founded one of Queens’ beloved Chinese restaurants. There's just one problem: She can't cook. So, she hits the road to learn from Asian American chefs, explore her culinary heritage and see if she can bring the family business back to life.Why it's worth your time: Watching Awkwafina get schooled in the kitchen is entertaining enough, but there's a surprisingly heartfelt story simmering underneath. As she travels from Texas barbecue joints to Hawaiian pig roasts, she meets chefs who've wrestled with their own family legacies and forged new paths in food. Where to watch: Apple TV

Genre: Historical action dramaWhat it’s about: In 1381 England, the Black Death has decimated the population, the surviving peasants are being squeezed by crushing taxes levied by King Richard II’s wealthy advisers. Enter Ploughman (Andrew Garfield), a farmer who rallies his fellow commoners into a full-scale rebellion against the crown. Joined by historical firebrands Wat Tyler (Cosmo Jarvis) and John Ball (Jamie Bell), the uprising marches toward London with one goal: justice for the people.Why you should watch it: “Jason Bourne” director Paul Greengrass brings his signature gritty, handheld intensity to a medieval revolt that feels uncomfortably relevant today. It’s a brutal tale of class warfare, political corruption and ordinary people finally reaching their breaking point. Turns out the more things change, the more peasants get screwed.Where to watch: Peacock

When she’s not watching TV and movies for work, she’s watching them for fun, seeing live music, writing songs, knitting and gardening.

#3270. I tested the RedMagic 12 Pro – and it’s the fastest Android I’ve ever seen

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Mobile OS > Android

If it's possible to release a flagship phone while at the same time making it appear more like a midrange phone, Red Magic has found a way.

RedMagic just announced the international launch of the RedMagic 12 Pro — its latest flagship phone. Typically, the company releases devices in China first and then slowly rolls them out to the rest of the world. This time around, the company knew it had a phone that could compete with other flagship devices.

Also: I’ve been a Google Pixel fan for years, but this $500 Android phone is giving me pause

RedMagic’s phones are high-performance devices known to do one thing especially well: mobile gaming. The RedMagic 12 Pro is no exception. It houses a Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 CPU with up to 5.01 GHz, which is paired with the RedMagic R5 Gaming Chipset, and I can honestly say it’s the fastest Android phone I’ve ever tested.

After the initial setup, I installed Geekbench 7 to benchmark the phone and compare it to my Pixel 9 Pro. As for the latest iPhone, according to Geekbench, the iPhone 18 Pro Max comes out ahead in single-core performance, but it just barely falls behind in multi-core performance.

The RedMagic 7 Pro nearly doubled the Pixel 11 Pro’s multi-core score. And Google’s device couldn’t beat the single-core score either. As I said, I’ve never seen a Geekbench score this high.

Real-world usage confirms these numbers, because the phone reacts faster and behaves more smoothly than any Android device I’ve owned or tested. It’s so smooth and fast, it feels like magic. But it’s not just the speed that makes this phone special.

First off, I’ve always liked RedMagic’s Android “skin.” As you use it, it seems to be some amalgamation of Android and iOS. RedMagic is essentially doing what Google’s been trying for years: making the smoothest possible animations on Android.

Also: I switched to an Android with liquid cooling for a week – now I wish every phone had it

The interface is as elegant as any I’ve seen on a mobile device. Pull down the notification shade, and it glides down like it was made of silk. Tap on an app launcher, and it opens immediately. Switch between apps, and there’s zero lag or jitter. On top of that, there’s hardly any bezel to speak of — the display goes nearly to the edge of the device.

There’s also no indication of where the front-facing camera is. There’s no pinhole (as you’ll find with many Android devices), and there’s no island (like on iPhones). It’s just a solid display with no interruptions.

The Pro 12 also feels really good in the hand. Both the back and the front are glass. Yes, it invites fingerprints, but it feels so smooth. The back of the phone also has that typical RedMagic look and feel with integrated RGB lighting zones. You can customize the lighting zones for things like fan on/off, game key atmosphere, media atmosphere, incoming calls, charging, and the alarm clock.

Also: This 15-inch portable monitor solved my big issue with cheaper models – and rivals my Mac display

Everything, and I mean everything, about this phone is fast.

The RedMagic 12 Pro is 100% a gaming phone. I installed “Diablo: Immortal” and found it to perform better than the last RedMagic gaming-specific tablet I tested. Not only was it fast, but the graphics were gorgeous. Crisp, smooth, and responsive.

Since the RedMagic 12 Pro is advertised as a serious gaming phone, why does it include preinstalled games that are decidedly non-serious?

On this powerful gaming phone, you’ll find apps like Puzzle Spark, Mahjong Blast, Bolt Twist, GoGo! Blast, and Little Kitty, Big City preinstalled. These are not serious games. In fact, these game titles sound more like they belong on a list of malicious apps (they aren’t).

Also: This 9-inch tablet singlehandedly changed my mind about gaming on Android

I would rather see the Red Magic 12 Pro have zero preinstalled games than the collection it ships with. Yes, you can easily delete those apps, but their being on the phone kind of cheapens it. Given how amazing this phone is, I think RedMagic could get away with shipping a bit less cheese, and a lot more wine.

Either way, the RedMagic 12 Pro is a phone that belongs at the top of the heap among flagships, even above every Pixel phone ever released. If there is a phone that can impress me more than the RedMagic 12 Pro, I’ve yet to see it.

#3269. Scientists Build Biocomputer That Runs on Bacteria to Solve Hard Problems

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The study relied on the bacterium E. coli and V. natriegens to run the calculations.

Move over, microchips. The next generation of supercomputing might just run on living bacteria. For 20 years, an international team of scientists has been developing a biocomputer that uses bacteria to process information. Scientists from McGill University in Montreal announced their findings on Nov. 3 and published a paper detailing the results earlier this year in Nature.

Researchers from Canada, Europe, the United Kingdom and Australia contributed to this work, which combines biology with computer science and engineering. The researchers say the resulting biocomputer could be used to solve problems that give standard computers a hard time.

“Electronic (sequential) computers are not meant, or designed, to solve decision trees,” Dan Nicolau, a McGill bioengineering professor and senior author for the research paper, told CNET via email.

Nicolau noted that if electronic computers are to solve these types of problems, the computers will need a lot of RAM.

The study relied on the bacterium Escherichia coli and Vibrio natriegens to run the calculations. The researchers used E. coli because it moves through fluid in a predictable, measurable way and V. natriegens because it reproduces very quickly.

By using live bacteria rather than digital processing, the team says the biocomputer can solve big, complex problems at a small fraction of the memory and resources that regular computers require.

The researchers tested the biocomputer with a seemingly simple math problem called the Subset Sum Problem, which famously becomes exponentially harder as the number of inputs increases.

When the Subset Sum Problem inputs grow too large, the problem is known to give traditional computers issues, such as taking centuries, or even millions of years, to solve the problem.

The researchers translated the problem into a graph that branches off into each possible combination of inputs. Next, the team created a tiny physical structure that mirrored the Subset Sum Problem graph.

Inside the structure, they built a network of tunnels to mirror the graph branches. Each fork in the tunnels represents a decision point, and every possible route through the tunnels represents a different solution to the problem.

The researchers unleashed bacteria, which rapidly reproduce, inside the tunnels. The fast-growing bacteria moved through the tunnels, exploring many routes to the solution simultaneously.

Compared to digital processing, the bacteria are slow. But rather than tackling a problem sequentially, as traditional computers do, the bacteria can examine many solutions at once. And if you need more computing power, bacterial reproduction within the tunnels creates additional processing units to help solve the problem.

The team used automated image analysis to follow the bacteria through the correct tunnels. In this way, the researchers were able to tell which paths through the network satisfied the problem’s constraints.

The researchers were also able to adjust temperatures to prevent bacteria overcrowding while traveling through the network.

Enterprising fans have figured out how to run Doom, the groundbreaking 1993 first-person shooter video game, on everything from E. coli to a thermostat. Nicolau says Doom could probably run on the new system, with an important caveat concerning the biocomputer’s size.

“(The biocomputer) must be huge!” Nicolau said. Because bacteria make slow processors, you would need a massive biocomputer to host enough bacteria to run a video game.

But because no RAM is needed, Nicolau said biocomputing could help to solve the global RAM shortage, and even broaden our understanding of what a computer could be.

“A computer is a device which accepts (input) numbers and gets out (output) numbers. Full stop,” he said. “All other uses of the word computer (are) from our point of view, well, poetical.”

I really wanted to love the Fitbit Edge, especially when I unboxed the cute pink version of Google’s latest tracker. I’m a huge fan of the $99 Fitbit Air, which launched earlier this year and immediately became one of the best screenless trackers on the market. Yet after two weeks of wearing the Fitbit Edge, I’m not convinced — here are three things I wish Google had done differently.

Before we dive in, you can read my colleague Dan’s extensive Fitbit Edge review here, as well as our Fitbit Air review on Tom’s Guide.

Let’s start with what I do like about the $180 Fitbit Edge. Firstly, I’m a fan of the design and fit of the tracker: it’s comfortable and unobtrusive on my wrist, especially compared to the likes of the Apple Watch Ultra 4 or Fenix 9 Pro, which I’ve recently been reviewing.

It’s dainty, and Google has done a fantastic job of releasing a huge range of swappable straps to suit every style. If you want a fitness tracker that’ll disappear, this isn’t quite as tiny as the Fitbit Air, but it still ticks that box.

I also think this device is pretty well priced. It’s $80 more than the Fitbit Air, but you’re getting a screen and built-in GPS. If you’re after a sports watch, I’d still recommend looking at something like the Coros Pace 4, which comes in at a similar price point, but for a fitness tracker, you’re getting a decent amount for your money with the Fitbit Edge.

Sure, it’s great to have a physical button on a fitness tracker, and this one is better than the haptic buttons we saw on the Fitbit Charge 6, but I’m a little frustrated by how little the Fitbit Edge’s button actually does.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

For example, you’d expect the button to start a run, not just stop it; instead, you still need to tap the screen before you start moving. Any runner knows nothing’s more frustrating than trying to swipe a touchscreen with sweaty fingers, especially on the start or finish line of a race.

The same applies to the stopwatch feature — you’d expect pressing the button would allow you to start the stopwatch, but instead it takes you back to the home screen. I’m never one to complain about a button on a wearable; in fact, the more buttons, the better, but I’m confused why the Fitbit Edge’s button doesn’t do an awful lot.

One thing missing from the Fitbit Edge compared to its predecessor, the Fitbit Charge 6, is contactless payments. Google says only 1% of Fitbit Charge 6 users utilized this feature, which is why they decided to remove it from the Fitbit Edge, but it still feels like a slightly odd decision in 2026.

Most people will be buying a fitness tracker to track their workouts, and I found a few things missing during my testing. Firstly, you can’t customize the data fields in workout modes or reorder them to see the ones most important to you. Again, this isn’t a deal breaker, but when the screen is that small, it would be nice to prioritize the data fields you care about most.

Secondly, I really wish you could do more when you’re on a walk or run. For example, you can’t use Google Maps navigation in workout modes, which is something I used pretty frequently when running or hiking around a new neighborhood. You also can’t control your music from the Fitbit Edge once you’re in a workout mode, which again, is something I didn’t realize I relied on until it was gone.

It’s also worth flagging that the GPS on the device is automatically set to dynamic, which means it switches between using your phone’s GPS and the built-in GPS. When you switch the tracker to using the built-in GPS, I found it takes a hit on battery life, using around 11% for an hour-long run.

It’s worth noting here that I’m probably not the target audience for the Fitbit Edge. The majority of people who buy this tracker won’t be using it for everyday runs or super-accurate GPS maps.

It’s designed for the casual fitness enthusiast who wants to keep an eye on their daily health metrics, and for that user, it does a great job. If you’re an endurance athlete or a serious runner, there are better devices on the market for you. Plus, if you’re not, a lot of these problems can be solved with a firmware update, so I wouldn’t let it put you off entirely.

#3265. Is Claude Code truly faster with message threads? I did the math on my logs

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Claude Code’s update could save you time during demanding, hours-long coding sessions at no extra cost. But by how much? Here's my real-world result.

Anthropic yesterday introduced message threads as part of Claude’s Messages API. Don’t confuse message threads with traditional human-to-human discussion threads. With message threads, entire conversations no longer have to be resent with each API call, saving roughly 35% of time-to-first-token when Claude requests contain 500,000 to 1 million tokens.

This feature is on by default for most Claude Code users. API users can turn it on using the “thread” parameter for API requests.

Token consumption remains unchanged, so this capability doesn’t provide a cost savings. The 35% savings is Anthropic’s measurement.

Also: Claude Code’s revised projects adds AI orchestration, but local developers must wait

Timing data from roughly 980 turns in my own Claude Code logs before this feature became available shows that Claude usually began a response about 3 seconds after each mid-task request when running contexts of 500,000 tokens and up. During five busy evenings last month, my conversations made roughly 100 to 225 model calls in a four hour stretch.

Using Anthropic’s reported 35% median time-to-first token reduction in a quick projection, Claude estimated a 2- to 4-minute savings per four hour work session.

Agents often send a bunch of requests to the model during each conversation. Before message threads, each message sent the entire conversation with each request.

Imagine if you’re in a very long texting chat with a friend. Now imagine if every time you sent a text to that friend, you also had to send every other text and every other reply along with that original text. That’s how model messaging has always worked. Except now, with message threads, there’s a better way.

Also: 75% of developers I surveyed prefer Claude Code – here’s why they choose it over Codex

With message threads turned on, agents only have to send what’s changed since the last turn. This reduces the amount of data transmission and increases responsiveness, what Anthropic calls time-to-first-token.

The benefit is seen most strongly in sessions that have a context of 500,000 to a 1 million tokens. About half of my sessions hit that context ceiling multiple times a night.

Anthropic reports that Claude’s message threads reduce median time-to-first-token by 35% for large requests. While my estimated savings of several minutes per session isn’t huge, the benefit increases with very long-running coding agents, and agents that transmit documents and image-heavy workloads.

For computer-using agents, all those screenshots “stay with the thread instead of being re-uploaded on every turn,” according to the Anthropic blog post on the feature.

Also: How I made a paid Mac app in 11 days with Claude – without writing a single line of code

While the time savings may not seem huge, in larger enterprise deployments or deployments where you want the AI to respond faster, any reduction in latency is a big deal and will be seen in any application of Claude technology that has a lot of back-and-forth turns with large data payloads.

Even though the addition of threads to the Messages API can reduce latency, token usage and therefore cost won’t go down. That’s because the model itself will still process the full conversation during every turn. Rate limits also don’t change.

Message threads and prompt caching can work together to reduce workload. Prompt caching has been around for about two years now, and it does save money. That’s because prompt caching allows the model to avoid re-processing prompts over and over (for example, in looping analysis calls).

On the other hand, the message threads capability does offer an extra smidge of performance, at no extra cost. So, there’s that.

Context is the size of the full session that Claude is currently working with. The rough human equivalent is current working or short-term memory. Most Claude Code sessions max out at a million token context, where a locally-hosted AI on my 128GB Mac Studio handles a context no bigger than 64K, or about 6% of the Claude Code context size.

Also: After the vibe-coding rush comes the debugging hangover

Compaction is a process where the AI attempts to reduce and eliminate extra information to fit the current session’s turns into the available context. An oversimplified analog is when you save a JPEG with quality turned way down in order to save space. You lose a lot of the visual fidelity, but you still get the main idea.

The larger the context you have, the longer you can go before the session has to initiate compaction. But there’s a gotcha. The larger the context you have, the more chance there is the model will lose track of what it’s working on or make reasoning errors.

Individual one-off requests also won’t see an improvement from message threads. Also, any conversation that delays longer than 5 minutes between turns will send the full message contents and not just the new stuff.

This feature doesn’t eliminate context management or compaction. But if your context is quite large, it will make responses a bit snappier.

Overall, message threads are a good thing, a solid if small innovation that increases responsiveness. While the feature doesn’t reduce costs, there’s also no additional cost for the additional performance, which is itself a win.

#3264. Data Center Backers Suffer Near-Total Midterm Defeats Across the Country

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

More than 40 voting initiatives yielded almost nothing but resistance to data-center projects.

The 2026 midterm election blue wave, which shifted the balance of power in Congress and across state races toward Democrats, can be seen as a repudiation of AI and the controversial data centers that provide its computing power. Data center proponents have heavily backed President Donald Trump and Republican candidates, underscored by xAI CEO Elon Musk investing hundreds of millions of dollars into Texas midterm campaigns to support the industry.

But in many parts of the country, voters didn’t need to make their voices on data centers heard through candidates. They had direct initiatives on the ballot this week that would decide whether data center projects would move ahead in their districts.

In line with a growing backlash against data centers and AI, voters supported about 40 election-day measures that would restrict the construction of new data centers, with only one result — in Harwood, North Dakota — favoring data center expansion.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

As broken down by the website Data Centers on the Ballot, Ohio had the most number of voting measures: 21, all of which were in favor of restrictions.

Maine, Illinois, Kansas, New Jersey, California, Florida, Nevada, North Dakota and Wisconsin were the other states with data center voting.

Six elections were held earlier in 2026 in California, Michigan, New Hampshire and Wisconsin, with all of them finding voters opposed to allowing data center builds to continue without new restrictions.

Not all the proposed restrictions were the same. In some elections, voters decided whether to impose a megawatt cap on data center energy use, while other measures addressed specific zoning issues or whether data center projects should require voter approval. Some proposed an outright ban on new data centers, and six of those were successful.

Polls by groups including Pew Research have found Americans have soured on data centers due to high electricity bills, water use and environmental concerns, among other reasons. It’s also hard to separate concerns about data centers from concerns about AI affecting jobs. AI has also become a divisive enough issue to affect midterm voting.

The election results were so bad for the industry that Politico declared data centers to be “the midterms’ other big loser” next to Republicans. Not only did voters enact additional restrictions on builds across the country, but data centers were mentioned in Democratic victory speeches.

“I do not work for data centers. I do not work for Wall Street. I work for you, I work for Ohio,” Senator-elect Sherrod Brown said in his victory speech Tuesday night.

USA Today reported that two mayors, one in Oklahoma and one in Ohio, were recalled after public backlash over proposed data centers.

The midterms might have longer-term effects for tech companies and data center firms. It’s likely that with Democratic control of Congress, there’ll be more scrutiny.

“Public policy is going to reflect public opinion, and there’s been a very substantial change in public opinion just over the last year,” Darrell West, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, told Politico.

Political headwinds from the midterms could lead local officials across the country to gain public favor by delaying or canceling data center projects or putting pressure on the companies behind them to offer more attractive deals to communities. The days of huge tax breaks and incentives for data centers could be coming to a close.

“Now, (communities) are pushing data centers to pay taxes, create their own power plants, pay for their use of electricity and water and contribute to local community resources like education funds,” The New York Times reported.

#3260. This clever banking scam keeps phishing by faking its own demise – how it works

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

You won't see the 'suspended' sign because it's not meant for you.

KELA researchers have exposed an active financial-scam infrastructure that hosts hundreds of fraudulent websites capable of faking their own suspensions to stay online. As of Oct. 25, 2026, 248 financial scam and phishing domains tied to 189 major US banks and financial services have been linked to the same infrastructure.

According to the cybersecurity firm’s report, published on Tuesday, the “Suspended” infrastructure operation runs websites that have cloned the official domains of victim organizations, with a particular focus on business banking. Many domains use the [keyword]-[bank].com format, slotting in keywords such as “secure,” “disable,” “protect,” and “cancel.”

Also: Beware of Bluetooth sniffers: How your favorite gadgets could be exposing your data

A handful of servers spread across two shared hosting providers run the backend of Suspended infrastructure, which has also been tied to phishing campaigns targeting cryptocurrency exchanges and government services in the UK, the Netherlands, Australia, and New Zealand. As a result, the researchers believe that either a single operator is behind the setup or that the server infrastructure is part of a wider phishing-as-a-service platform.

This phishing campaign stands out because of how the cybercriminals behind the scam are protecting it: by issuing takedown notices.

When you visit a website and see a message that it has been taken down or suspended, it’s usually because the domain has been associated with malicious or illegal activity, including phishing and scams. Law enforcement agencies, often with help from technology firms, find these websites, obtain the necessary court orders, and seize the infrastructure or accounts behind them to force a suspension through a registrar or hosting provider.

You see the notice, you move on — and this also goes for scanners and security teams.

However, in this case, the scam artists created a mechanism to show it themselves, to avoid being flagged and taken down. But it’s when they show it that matters.

The false suspension notice appears deceptively simple at first glance. A phishing kit embedded in the domain registers the IP address of each visitor, and on their second visit, they are shown a fake “account suspended” page. The kit is disguised as a challenge page similar to those legitimately used by Cloudflare.

Researchers also detected other decoys, including “Sorry, you’ve been blocked” notices, blank pages, and redirections to Google. Some pages also have reCAPTCHAs, and the researchers detected scripts that block browser developer tools, likely to slow analysis.

Also: Don’t use Muse? Meta’s AI agent can still access your private messages – here’s how

But why show fake suspension notices in the first place? To scanners and cybersecurity teams, it looks like someone else has already dealt with the malicious domain, and they can move on to the next suspicious website.

“That design targets exactly the people who could shut a site down,” KELA says. “A victim typically follows a link once. A scanner, a security team or a takedown provider checks a reported site and then checks it again to confirm, and the second check shows what looks like a completed takedown.”

As shown in the image below, while scanners would detect a suspension notice, victims would still see the cloned website, complete with lures to entice them into entering their information, leading to financial fraud and potentially identity theft. After all, one visit is enough.

As of this writing, there are 248 live domains, plus those taken offline after the researchers disclosed their findings to law enforcement; over 300 scam domains have been hosted on the same infrastructure since May this year. Unfortunately, this phishing campaign remains active, with new domains appearing every day.

One lead could reveal the operator: a remote desktop connection to the malicious infrastructure through a standard UK home broadband connection, but it has not been verified.

Use a phishing link checker to verify whether a URL is trustworthy, and remember that any email or message claiming to be from your bank may be fraudulent.

Typical signs of a bank phishing email include:

When it comes to organizations, KELA has released a free Bank Phishing Check tool that compares official domains and organizations against the websites uncovered during the firm’s research.

#3257. 2 Dividend Stocks to Buy in November and 1 to Leave on the Shelf

The products that Coca-Cola and WD-40 sell may not be exciting, but their steady sales and profitability help those companies deliver reliable dividends.

With 2026 soon to be in the rearview mirror, some investors may be getting a head start on their portfolio reviews. Sometimes, such an analysis will reveal the need for just a little bit of rebalancing. Other times, a more comprehensive overhaul may be called for if, for example, an investor finds that a single sector now accounts for too large a slice of their portfolio, or if their investing goals have changed.

No matter what the case may be, it's never too early to ask yourself if there are enough dividend-paying stocks in your portfolio. Younger investors can consider taking advantage of dividend reinvestment plans (DRIPs), which seamlessly route dividend payouts into the purchase of additional shares of stock -- a strategy that gradually builds you a larger position in that company. Those added shares mean you collect even more in dividends to buy still more shares in a compound growth cycle.

And eventually, when you need to make use of the income from your portfolio, you can simply turn off the DRIP and start collecting those larger dividend payouts. For older investors, dividends can be a reliable monthly or quarterly source of income, depending on how frequently the company distributes them.

Whether or not we have income sources like that will eventually become an important issue for most of us, as research from The Motley Fool shows a worrying trend of retirees overrelying on Social Security. It found that, among retirees over 65, the most common source of income is Social Security, with 91% listing it as a source of income, based on data collected by the Federal Reserve in 2025. In comparison, only 54% of retirees over 65 listed interest, dividends, or rental income as a source of cash generation. Moreover, among all retirees, 58% described Social Security as a "major" source of their retirement income. The percentages describing any stock-based assets as major sources of retirement income were much lower than that.

"Social Security is not designed to be the sole source of income in retirement, which makes it worrisome that more retirees aren't tapping into other sources of money," The Motley Fool research report says.

That's why today, we'll look at two stocks that can be strong picks for income generation: Coca-Cola (KO -0.07%) and WD-40 (WDFC -2.43%). And while a stock with a high yield is always tempting, we'll also look at one high-yield name to avoid: Nike (NKE -2.30%).

The broader markets have wobbled at several points this year for reasons ranging from fears of an artificial intelligence bubble to concerns over stubborn inflation to uncertainty about where the Federal Reserve was leaning on interest rates. That said, despite all the uncertainty, both Coca-Cola and WD-40 have held up well this year. While the S&P 500 index is up 7.8% thus far in 2026, WD-40 stock has climbed 16.4%, and Coca-Cola shares have fared even better, rising 37%.

There are many reasons someone would want to own each stock individually. Still, generally speaking, it appears the market is giving a broad nod of approval to two companies with businesses built to last and business models that can withstand periods of uncertainty.

While neither business makes things that people can't live without, they make products that people need or want and will keep buying, even when budgets get tighter. Whether it's locked mechanisms in lawn tools or jammed Lego blocks, most people don't think twice about picking up a classic can of WD-40 spray lubricant.

A similar argument applies to Coca-Cola. Its offerings are not necessities. Still, a favorite soda, workout drink, or other Coca-Cola beverage can keep finding its way into shopping carts during weekly grocery runs, as these are the sorts of smaller indulgences that many people won't give up.

Granted, spray lubricants and sodas aren't the most exciting of products, but what's important is that they generate substantial profits for each company, which they can then use to pay dividends to shareholders. In its fiscal 2026 (which ended Aug. 31), WD-40 generated $82.1 million in net income, while Coca-Cola generated $4 billion in net income in the third quarter alone. Their reliable businesses have allowed WD-40 to pay dividends uninterrupted for over 40 years, and helped Coca-Cola earn the title of Dividend King. The beverage giant has increased its payouts annually for 64 consecutive years, well beyond the 50-year streak required to earn entry into that exclusive club.

WD-40's dividend yield is 1.8%, and Coca-Cola's is 2.2% -- not the highest in the consumer stock space by any stretch. But the benefit is that their payouts have been proven reliable, and those two reliable companies have also delivered recent stock price outperformance, boosting their total returns.

And that point brings us to the dividend stock it would be better to watch from afar: Nike.

Nike is quietly on the path to becoming known for being more of an income stock, having increased its dividend payouts for 24 consecutive years. Another attractive aspect of Nike as an investment is its dividend yield, which at the current share price is 4.2%.

That said, I'd put it on a watch list rather than buy it outright in November. Nike forecasts its revenue will fall by a high-single-digit percentage in 2027, and it's still struggling to revitalize its iconic brands even as it experiences a sales slump in the Greater China market. All of that contributed to its stock price woes over the last 12 months, with shares falling 38%.

I'd want to see positive sales momentum before investing in the athletic apparel giant, as that could help stabilize its stock price and increase Nike's reliability as a dividend payer. But if the stock price keeps falling, that's going to cut into your total returns or even result in losses, regardless of those dividend payouts. That's why, even if their yields are lower, I'd still rather own Coca-Cola and WD-40 because of the stability and reliability they offer.

Jack Delaney has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Nike. The Motley Fool recommends WD-40. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

Aside from the best foldable phones, I tend to see a lot of innovation around rugged phones built for long-term off-grid living or weekend camping getaways.

I’ve tested my fair share of unconventional ones: from the projector-packing Blackview Xplore 2 all the way to the Sonim XP Pro Thermal with its Predator-like heat vision. Every single one brought something wild to the table, but the Oukitel WP63 packs something I genuinely haven't seen before: a built-in electronic fire igniter.

While most phone manufacturers design their hardware specifically to avoid catching fire (ahem, Note 7), this heavy-duty slab embraces it for emergency survival. Honestly, it’s one of the most interesting rugged phones I’ve come across this year.

If the igniter alone isn’t enough to convince you, it also packs a massive 20,000mAh battery, a built-in reverse-charging cable, an all-in-one camping lantern, and a night vision camera.

Best of all, it’s currently 43% off for a limited time, dropping the price from $599 down to $339.

Built for extreme off-grid adventures, the Oukitel WP63 features an emergency electronic fire igniter, massive 20,000 mAh battery, built-in reverse-charging cable, 6.67-inch 120Hz display, rear camping lantern, and an 8MP night vision camera to see through the darkness.

The integrated lighter on the Oukitel WP63 brings back memories of the push-in cigarette lighters found in old-school cars. The heating element is tucked away on the top edge of the phone, popping open to reveal the recessed coil with a light press. Through the dedicated Lighter app, I can trigger the ignition process, which quickly causes the coil to glow with that familiar cherry-red warmth.

It generates concentrated heat capable of sparking dry materials on direct contact — like scrap paper or dried-up leaves that have been baking under the sun. For safety reasons, the igniter enforces an automatic cooldown period of around 10 seconds to prevent the housing from overheating.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

While I was genuinely surprised by how easily it lit the corner of an envelope, keep in mind that nursing that spark into a sustainable fire takes real effort. Because it doesn’t produce an open flame like a Bic lighter or butane torch, having prior campfire-building experience makes a huge difference. After several tries, I managed to get a small bundle of brittle autumn leaves to catch, but it definitely requires patience and bone-dry kindling.

Beyond its standard 64MP main shooter — which delivers respectable shots when lighting conditions cooperate — Oukitel also throws in a dedicated 8MP infrared night vision camera. For a rugged phone built for the backcountry, it’s an invaluable tool the moment true darkness sets in.

While dedicated night vision cameras I’ve tested offer superior performance, especially in how far their IR illuminators can reach, the WP63’s sensor is still ideal for scanning your immediate vicinity for critters rustling in the brush. If you're out camping, it's especially handy when you have to step out of your tent half-asleep in the dead of night and your eyes haven't yet adjusted to the blackness.

Even though the setup is limited to just a single main camera and a night vision lens, the quality from the primary sensor more than suffices for the quick run-and-gun shots I want to share on social media. And the selfie camera up front isn’t too shabby, either.

As much as I rely on the flashlight on my phones, they’re dinky compared to the blinding beam produced by the WP63’s rear-mounted camping light. At its brightest, it effortlessly illuminates an entire pitch-dark area, and it has serious endurance thanks to the massive 20,000 mAh battery packed inside. With hurricane season in full swing, I’m confident it could easily hold up through an extended power outage. On top of that, an emergency strobe function unleashes an intense beacon that can be spotted from long distances.

I also want to highlight the 3W loudspeaker mounted on the back, which completely puts flagship phone audio to shame. While most phones tend to distort heavily at maximum volume, this speaker delivers surprising low-end punch and clarity — making it feel like I’m carrying a dedicated Bluetooth speaker in my pocket.

The Oukitel WP63 is an unlocked phone ready to run on virtually any wireless carrier, and I love that it features one of the easiest SIM card slots to access without hunting down an ejector pin.

This Swiss Army knife approach works because it nails the practical essentials for off the grid excursions — headlined by its halo feature, the built-in igniter. That utility is backed by smart additions like an integrated USB-C cable, allowing it to double as a ready-to-go power bank for other gear.

Tipping the scales at over 1.3 pounds, it’s certainly not a device I’d want as my primary everyday carry. But as a secondary backup? It’s an easy sell, especially while it's 43% off. Whether you toss it into a glove compartment for road trips or pack it along for a weekend in the woods, the Oukitel WP63 delivers rugged peace of mind when facing worst-case scenarios.

#3250. Here's What $5,000 in USA Rare Earth Could Be Worth by 2030 If It Reaches MP Materials' Market Cap

USA Rare Earth is investing heavily in building its mine-to-magnet supply chain.

The United States is looking to break China's stronghold on rare-earth mining and processing. MP Materials (MP -6.04%) and USA Rare Earth (USAR -9.51%) are two publicly traded companies with government support to build a domestically controlled "mine-to-magnet" supply chain.

MP Materials, which already owns the Mountain Pass mine in California, is a leader in the space and has a market capitalization of around $6.7 billion. USA Rare Earth's market cap is roughly half that size at $3.3 billion.

For USA Rare Earth to reach MP Materials' market cap by 2030, its stock would have to more than double from here, turning a $5,000 investment into over $10,150. Here's what has to go right for USA Rare Earth to achieve this.

Unlike MP Materials, which owns the largest rare-earth mine in North America, USA Rare Earth is building its entire supply chain from scratch. As part of establishing its mine-to-magnet supply chain, the company has invested heavily to acquire Serra Verde, which gives it upstream mining assets and the only large-scale rare-earth mine outside China that contains all four critical magnet minerals.

On top of that, the company has acquired downstream assets, including Less Common Metals, which gives it a specialist in turning rare earth into high-grade metals and alloys. The company is also expanding its permanent magnet production capabilities in Oklahoma and building a new facility in South Carolina.

For USA Rare Earth to deliver strong returns for investors, it must successfully integrate its acquisitions while scaling its processing and manufacturing capabilities.

With Serra Verde and its Round Top Project in Texas, USA Rare Earth has an opportunity to become a leading domestic supplier of heavy rare-earth elements (HREEs), a capability MP Materials currently lacks.

That said, developing and integrating all of these assets is no easy feat, making USA Rare Earth a higher-risk stock to play the build-out of the U.S. mine-to-magnet supply chain.

#3249. Windows 11 can run better on PCs with 8GB now, Microsoft says – here’s why

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Windows > Windows 11

The latest updates to Windows 11 offer improvements in speed, performance, and memory management.

The more memory your Windows PC has, the faster it should perform, especially when juggling multiple apps, files, and other data. My laptop has 32GB of RAM, while my desktop has a hefty 64GB, and both are absolutely zippy. Does that mean computers with only 8GB of memory, or even less, are also-rans? Nope, not according to Microsoft.

Also: How much RAM does your PC really need?

In a new blog post published Tuesday, Microsoft touted the gains in speed, performance, and memory management in Windows 11 achieved by the latest updates. These especially impact PCs with just 8GB of RAM, which can now run multiple apps and files faster and more efficiently than before.

To reach this goal, the company said it had three notions in mind.

The first was to make better use of the existing memory on each Windows 11 PC. The second was to protect the tasks that need to feel instant even as more memory gets used. And the third was to ensure that key apps and Windows require less memory. Yes, a computer with 16GB, 32GB, or 64GB of RAM can better handle more intensive activities. But Microsoft wanted to make sure that systems with 8GB could also keep pace.

Based on its own lab tests of PCs with 8GB of RAM, the company claims that Windows is now 20% more responsive and that multitasking is 40% faster than before the latest updates. Here’s how.

As more memory gets allocated, Windows must move inactive apps and files from RAM to the hard drive. When you need to access those apps and files again, you have to wait for Windows to move them from disk storage back to RAM. Normally, PCs with less memory have to do a lot of this disk swapping.

One way Windows eases the pain of this process is through compression. Here, the operating system shrinks less-active data into a smaller format so it can remain in memory. Though Windows has used compression for many years, Microsoft has fine-tuned the technology to determine how much to compress, when to move data from RAM to your drive, and when to fetch it back, especially on PCs with 8GB of memory.

Also: 5 apps I always install on new Windows PCs – most are free

As such, Windows can now keep up to 2GB more of your active data in memory rather than moving it to storage, Microsoft said. An inactive app, file, or browser that you leave open is less likely to have to reload from your hard drive when you return to it.

Opening the Start menu, launching File Explorer, right-clicking a folder or file, and searching for an item are all tasks that need to feel instant; otherwise, Windows itself feels sluggish. To achieve this on PCs with less RAM, Windows tries to prioritize certain actions you need to accomplish while backing off background tasks like search indexing, Microsoft said.

Here’s one example. After you update your computer and reboot, Windows has some housekeeping to do. But any setup work that occurs shouldn’t affect how long it takes to open an app or file.

Also: How to upgrade your ‘incompatible’ Windows 10 PC to Windows 11 – for free

The latest version of Windows 11 speeds up these types of tasks and interactions by up to 20% compared with the January 2026 version, according to Microsoft.

However, multitasking places the greatest strain on a PC with only 8GB of RAM. To analyze this, Microsoft said it conducted two tests on the same PC with 8GB of memory. One test measured the current version of Windows 11, while the other gauged the January 2026 flavor. Here, the testers opened 20 tabs in Microsoft Edge, kicked off a 4K video, and launched large files in Word, PowerPoint, and Excel, one after another. The current version of Windows is up to 40% faster than its predecessor, the company said.

To reduce the need for RAM among Windows and certain key apps, Microsoft said that it has improved how memory is managed and when it’s used.

As one example, memory is allocated to Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and Outlook more efficiently, resulting in a 360 MB savings in RAM. This maneuver also extends to third-party apps such as WhatsApp, which has reduced its memory requirements.

Also: 11 Windows apps I replace on every new PC (and the ones I keep)

On PCs with 8GB of memory, the Widgets app loads only when you open it and frees up about 200 MB of RAM when you close it. In Microsoft Edge, inactive tabs now go to sleep after 15 minutes, down from two hours previously, reducing overall memory allocation.

Across Windows, Microsoft 365, and Edge, those improvements reduced the growth in required memory by up to 900 MB, Microsoft said.

How does Microsoft test these scenarios to see whether the latest Windows updates and fixes are helping PCs with less memory?

“We test those fixes across a broader collection of over 20,000 PCs in our labs, including current 8 GB models, using automated workloads based on activities such as browsing, working in Microsoft 365 apps, joining video calls, and downloading files in the background and even using high-speed cameras to measure the time from an action, such as opening Start or launching an app, to the moment the result appears on screen,” the company explained.

Also: Why your RAM options cost 4X more now than last year

The ability to use Windows without much RAM on your PC is critical these days in light of the “RAMageddon” crisis. With AI companies scooping up massive amounts of memory and flash storage chips, remaining supply is limited, and the prices have surged. The more memory you add to a new or existing PC, the more you’re going to pay. That’s always been true, but now more than ever.

Of course, memory is only one part of the picture. Your PC’s processor and other hardware also play an important role. Here, Microsoft found that a 2026 Dell XPS 13 with 8GB of RAM showed 94% faster multi-core CPU performance than a 2021 8 GB model. But the same 2026 8GB PC performed on par with a 2021 16 GB system. This shows that memory does matter for multitasking, but that the processor also impacts performance.

Whether your Windows 11 PC has 8GB of RAM, less, or more, how can you take advantage of the latest enhancements? For that, you’ll want to make sure that you’ve updated to the newest version of Windows. That would be Windows 11 26H2, build 26300.9818 or later, according to Microsoft. But that includes the latest optional preview build released in late October. If you don’t want to install that one, you’ll be fine with build 26300.9711 for now.

Also: The best laptops: Expert tested and reviewed

To check, head to Settings, select System, and then click About. The section for Windows Info shows the current version and build. If you need to update, stay in Settings and go to Windows Update. Assuming your PC qualifies, you should find the latest Windows 11 26H2 build ready to install.

Beyond updating Windows, you also want to keep your apps current. If you use Microsoft 365, open any app in the suite, click the File menu, select Account, click Update Options, then select Update Now.

With most other apps, you have to update them manually or individually. To ease the process, consider a good software updater program. These will automatically scan most of your installed applications to identify which need updating, then download and install the updates for you.
